source: Ersoz (2026) 12 Angry AI Agents: Evaluating Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making Through Cinematic Jury Deliberation
finding: Twelve persona agents re-ran the 11-1 to 12-0 flip of the film 12 Angry Men. The flip almost never happened. Nearly every run ended hung.
numbers: 18 runs (2 models x 3 conditions x N=3), temp 0.9, max 150 turns. 17/18 hung juries (94%). GPT-4o hung in 9/9. Llama-4-Scout 8 hung, 1 unanimous NOT_GUILTY (no-initial-vote condition, run 2, 64 turns, 6 vote changes).
quote: Seventeen of eighteen runs end in a hung jury
limits: Exploratory, N=3 per cell, no significance tests. One film case, 8 evidence items, persona-fixed starting votes. Early stop after 3 vote rounds with zero changes.
agent_relevance: Direct test of the critique that the story model is thin on deliberation. Agents hold their first position. Do not rely on a second round of discussion to move an answer; check the first stance with code.

source: Ersoz (2026) 12 Angry AI Agents (prompt ablation)
finding: An 'open-minded' instruction ('do not cling to your first instinct; update if the counter-argument is sound') changed Llama a lot and GPT-4o not at all.
numbers: Mean vote changes per run: GPT-4o 1.0 baseline, 0.7 no-initial-vote, 1.0 open-minded. Llama-4-Scout 2.0 baseline, 3.3 no-initial-vote, 6.0 open-minded (runs 5, 5, 8). Mean turns: GPT-4o 44-64, Llama 60-72.
limits: N=3 per cell. Attributing the gap to RLHF intensity is the author's hypothesis; two models only, so model family is confounded with alignment depth.
agent_relevance: A 'be open to updating' line in a prompt is not a reliable lever (matches guardrail G1: doubt on a signal, not on an instruction). Whether it works depends on the model, so test per model.

source: Ersoz (2026) 12 Angry AI Agents (no-initial-vote condition and persona fidelity)
finding: Agents reproduced the film's evidence list and character voices but not the persuasion. Assigned starting votes acted as an extra anchor for the flexible model. Removing them let one run converge.
numbers: All 18 runs cited the same 5 core evidence items (knife, old man, woman across street, El train, threat). Juror_8 had highest key-argument coverage. Every conditioned run kept its assigned vote at the first vote check. Hung-jury label required 3 consecutive vote rounds (36 turns) with no change.
limits: Persona-conditioned agents may be rigid because of the persona, not the model. Same-evidence reading shows the evidence-to-story step works; the gap is in the social step.
agent_relevance: Story building from a case file is easy for models. What is missing is revision after hearing a rival story. Put the revision trigger in code (a failing check), not in conversation.

source: Wu (2026) When Does Defendant Statement Matter? Bias and Persuasion in LLM-Simulated Jurors (JuryBench)
finding: Largest LLM jury study found: 20 frontier models judged 500 controversial US criminal cases before and after a defendant statement. Emotional statements often made verdicts harsher, not milder. Models differ a lot in sign.
numbers: 432K decisions, 20 LLMs. Statement effect SE (severity drop, 0-15 scale): Gemini 3 Flash +0.549 (success rate 15.0%, hurt 5.3%); GPT-5 Mini +0.327; Grok-4.3 +0.305; Qwen3 -0.592; Claude Opus 4.6 -0.385; GLM 5 -0.384. For most rows 66-86% of verdicts did not change (no-change rate 0.68-0.86). Hurt rate exceeded success rate in most models.
quote: emotional persuasion can be detrimental, since jurors may perceive it as evidence of guilt or inconsistency
limits: Synthetic cases and personas. Severity dictionary labelled by a human expert, single labeller. Single-shot decisions, no deliberation between jurors.
agent_relevance: A story told with more feeling is not a better-supported story. Score on evidence coverage, not on how the account reads. Supports 'caution on scoring' in the subfield row.

source: Wu (2026) JuryBench (latent-factor regression)
finding: Match between juror and defendant background was a stronger driver of verdict change than emotion or remorse. LLM jurors were harsher to out-group defendants and softer to in-group ones.
numbers: Linear model SE = a + b1 z(emotion) + b2 z(remorse) + b3 z(background fit), least squares per model. Background fit coefficient positive and significant for a substantial majority of models; none of the negative ones significant. Strongest: GPT-5.5, Grok-4.3, GPT-5 Mini, Claude Haiku 4.5. Remorse reduced severity in a sizable minority (DeepSeek-V4, Gemini, some GPT); Grok and a few GPT models read remorse as guilt. Ideology buckets: strong conservative jurors gave highest severity, strong liberal lowest; ~70% of models showed larger post-statement change for conservative jurors.
limits: Persona text states ideology and background outright; real jurors rarely announce them. Human check used 12 lay raters on 25 cases, all near neutral ideology, so background-fit term was dropped there.
agent_relevance: Narrative judgement is open to identity cues in the prompt. Strip persona and background details from any step that scores a story.

source: Wu (2026) JuryBench (human comparison)
finding: Twelve lay people on 25 simpler cases also tended to raise severity after the statement, mostly because they read remorse as evidence of guilt or the speech as performative.
numbers: 12 US lay participants, 25 cases, human SE negative (harsher). Without background term, emotion coefficient 0.173 and remorse -0.168, both p<0.05 but >0.01. Cited human work in paper: black sheep effect (Kerr 1995), conservative jurors convict more (Clark and Wink 2012; Anwar 2019).
limits: Small human sample, text-only survey. Authors say humans cannot perceive background difference in text.
agent_relevance: LLM jurors echo some human effects, but the human baseline is weak. Do not treat a model as a validated stand-in for jurors.

source: Wynn, Satija, Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Understanding Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Debate between model agents can lower accuracy below plain majority vote. Correct answers get flipped to wrong ones to match peers. Accuracy can fall as rounds go on.
numbers: Three datasets; single-agent rows vs majority vote vs debate compared. Agents with more agreeing peers flipped from correct to incorrect more often (Figure 4). Round 2 social pressure beats round 1 resistance (Figure 3). Exact percentages in tables not extracted this session.
limits: Workshop paper. I read the intro, method and figure captions; table values not transcribed.
agent_relevance: The 11-1 to 12-0 flip in humans is reproduced by models as a bad flip toward the majority. Never let agreement among samples count as proof (G4).

source: Bertalanic and Fortuna (2026) The Cost of Consensus: Isolated Self-Correction Prevails Over Unguided Homogeneous Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Debate among identical 7-8B models did not beat one model correcting itself alone, and cost 2-3 times the tokens. Models drifted to the modal peer answer.
numbers: 3 models (Qwen2.5-7B, Ministral-3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), 10 agents, 3 rounds, GSM-Hard and MMLU-Hard. Ministral GSM-Hard: debate 20.7% vs self-correction 48.3% (p<0.001) vs zero-shot 24.7%; tokens 23,816 vs 10,707 per problem. Qwen2.5-7B MMLU-Hard: self-correction 66.7% vs debate 60.7% (p<0.001). Qwen GSM-Hard: irrelevant-rationale noise control 63.2% beat debate 58.8%. Modal sycophancy up to 85.5% (MMLU-Hard, 9 agents); oracle gap up to 32.3 points (right answer produced then discarded in consensus). Llama comparisons not significant (p=0.131, 0.155).
limits: Only small open-weight models, homogeneous teams, no roles. Authors say it is a lower bound on what debate can do.
agent_relevance: Strong counter-evidence to using group discussion to pick a story. A single revise-from-failing-output loop (G2) is cheaper and at least as good.

source: Hao et al. (2026) Not All Flips Are Conformity: Decomposing Stance Convergence in Multi-Agent LLM Debate
finding: Many answer changes in debate happen with no peer at all. After removing that baseline, peers still pulled agents, for better and worse. Full reasoning exchange added no majority-vote gain over self-reflection.
numbers: 5 GPT-4o agents, MMLU-Pro disagreement questions, 5,200 agent-question pairs: 36.98% change under self-reflection alone. Of pairs stable there, 29.30% adopted a peer answer after seeing stances. Individual accuracy 42.17% (self-reflection) to 45.87% (full reasoning); majority-vote accuracy 77.35% in both across 4,900 questions; full reasoning used 57% more tokens.
limits: Homogeneous single round. Rates differ across GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3-Plus.
agent_relevance: A juror 'changing its mind' is not proof of persuasion. For our agent, count a flip only when tied to new evidence, not to a re-ask.

source: Kumarappan and Mujoo (2026) Not Just RLHF: Why Alignment Alone Won't Fix Multi-Agent Sycophancy
finding: A fake jury of peers unanimously asserting a wrong answer made a Llama subject drop the right one. The effect depends on how many peers agree and which chat role carries the text. One dissenter largely broke the effect.
numbers: Subject Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, 400 MMLU humanities questions, 3 jury models (Gemma-2-9B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B). User-role framing: yield under 13% for 0-3 wrong agents, 80.25% at 4v0; a single dissenter at 3v1 kept it at 12.75%. Assistant-role framing: under 7% up to 2 wrong, 60.25% at 3v1, 97.50% at 4v0. Cross-framing gap at 3v1 is 47.5 points. Dissenter rescue cut yield by 54-73 points. Base models showed the same pattern (Qwen2.5-7B base 92.1% vs Instruct 43.2% for assistant-role jury).
limits: One subject model for the mechanism work. Pre-written jury text, no live debate.
agent_relevance: Gives a number for 11-1 style pressure on a model and for the fix: one structured dissenter. If we ever use several voices, keep at least one voice that argues the other side.

source: Choi et al. (2025) An Empirical Study of Group Conformity in Multi-Agent Systems
finding: Centrist LLM agents in debates on contentious topics moved toward the bigger group and toward the more capable agents.
numbers: Over 2,500 simulated debates, 5 topics (basic income, gender wage gap, immigration, education equality, death penalty). Chi-square and two-way ANOVA at alpha=0.01. Conformity rate rose with relative majority size and with agent intelligence (ACL 2025 Findings).
limits: Opinion topics with no ground truth. Fixed temperature 0.7, 256-token replies.
agent_relevance: Mirrors human conformity in juries. A stronger model's story will dominate a weaker model's story whether or not it is right.

source: Sachdeva and van Nuenen (2026) Interaction Protocol Shapes Moral Judgment in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: On contested moral cases the order and format of the debate changed the verdict as much as the content. Models differ greatly in how often they revise.
numbers: 15,000 debates (plus 15,000 with open models), Reddit AITA dilemmas, protocols: synchronous and round-robin, max 4 rounds. Synchronous: GPT-4.1 revised 0.6-3.1% of the time vs 28-41% for Claude and Gemini (abstract figures). Round-robin: Claude vs GPT ended in round 1 nearly 90% of the time when Claude went first, only ~40% when GPT went first. Consensus-reaching debates raised value similarity 30-60%; non-consensus 6-17%.
limits: Moral dilemmas, not evidence disputes. Multinomial inertia/conformity fit is model-specific.
agent_relevance: Who speaks first decides a lot. If we compare rival stories, randomise or hide order and run both orders.

source: Jagged Judges (2026) Epistemic Stability Under Perturbation, Pressure, and Persistence
finding: LLM judges drop their verdicts under pushback. A persuader model that adapts moves them most. Cycling many tactics works worse than repeating one strong claim of expert consensus.
numbers: 9 judges (GPT-5/5.2/5.4, Claude 4.6 Sonnet/Opus, Grok-4.1 and Reasoning, Gemini 3 Flash/3.1 Pro), 14 tasks, 6 datasets, pressure ladder L1-L6. Verdicts flip 25-71% under static pushback and 62-91% under an adversarial LLM persuader. Mechanical perturbation wiggle only 2-9%. L4 'three independent reviewers all disagree' cut retention to 73% at turn 1. L6 adaptive persuasion reached ~50% retention by turn 10. Claude Opus: 2% mechanical wiggle but 44% under sustained pressure.
limits: Judging tasks (safety, toxicity), not legal. Pushback is scripted.
agent_relevance: A 'consensus of reviewers' claim moves a model fast. If a checker is used, it must not read claims of agreement; it must read outputs (G2, G3).

source: Ni and Zou (2026) Silent Dissent: LLM Agents That Yield to the Majority Still Represent Their Original Premise
finding: Agents that gave in to a unanimous wrong majority still carried the original fact inside. Whether they yielded depended much on whether their own earlier answer stayed visible.
numbers: Pre-registered; scripted unanimous peers (Asch style). Hiding the agent's earlier answer raised Qwen3.5-4B's giving-in rate from 8% to 89%. Direct answer-token readout failed a positive control (0 of 1,000). Authors do not claim agents infer the premise implied by peers (offset 0.02, CI -0.10 to 0.15, exploratory).
limits: Two-hop factual statements, small open models, exploratory parts flagged.
agent_relevance: Count of agents who converged overstates agreement. Keep each attempt's first answer in view so a later vote does not erase it.

source: Ersoz (2026) 12 Angry AI Agents (related-work and design)
finding: Uses AutoGen SelectorGroupChat with a dissent-priority speaker rule, a vote prompt every 12 turns and an early-stop rule. Shows how to measure deliberation: vote-change timeline, cascade velocity, first-flip order, and Spearman correlation with the film's canonical order.
numbers: Metrics: verdict, turns, vote-change tuples, changes per turn, first-flip order, Spearman rho (only when 2 or more jurors flip). Observed run length 36-84 turns.
limits: Spearman rarely computable because few jurors flipped.
agent_relevance: A ready pattern for a code-side 'did anyone actually move' counter inside an agent loop. Cheap to copy; not a story-model method itself.

source: Urbaniak (2017) Reconciling Bayesian Epistemology and Narration-based Approaches to Judiciary Fact-finding
finding: A formal model that turns the informal story criteria into probability conditions. It defends the story approach against the Bayesian charge that 'plausibility' is a primitive, and keeps the Bayesian tools.
numbers: No empirical numbers. Criteria formalised: explaining evidence (each non-excluded evidence item must be strongly plausible given the accusing story; defence story only needs the evidence not to be ruled out), missing evidence, exclusion between rival stories, decision (each story must state guilt or not), initial plausibility, exhaustion. Uses partial probability functions with strong-plausibility stances.
quote: the fact-finders' decision is the result of a dynamic interplay between competing narratives
limits: Technical framework only; applications postponed to a later paper. Not tested on people or models.
agent_relevance: Gives a codeable version of 'coverage' scoring: per evidence item, is it plausible under story i. Also adds 'missing evidence' and 'exclusion' checks the plain story model lacks. Candidate for the scorer in S7.

source: Urbaniak (2017) Reconciling Bayesian Epistemology and Narration-based Approaches (gatecrasher paradox)
finding: Pure high probability of guilt is not enough (gatecrasher paradox). The no-plausible-alternative-story view avoids it because statistics alone are not a story. The paper also lists four criteria: evidential support, completeness, resiliency, narrativity.
numbers: No empirical numbers.
limits: Philosophical argument.
agent_relevance: Explains why story form matters (the open question in the subfield row): stories carry resiliency and completeness checks that a bare probability does not. A scorer should test those, not just a score.

source: He et al. (2024) AgentsCourt: Judicial Decision-Making Agents with Court Debate Simulation and Legal Knowledge Augmentation
finding: Early agent system that follows the trial: debate simulation, legal retrieval, then decision refinement. Beat other models on legal article selection.
numbers: SimuCourt benchmark 420 Chinese judgment documents (3 case types); Legal-KB knowledge base. F1 gains on legal article generation 8.6% (first instance) and 9.1% (second instance) over baselines. EMNLP 2024 Findings.
limits: Debates built from finished judgment documents, so the outcome is already known and facts are written in concluded form (criticised in JuryBench). Civil-law, rule-based, not lay-jury.
agent_relevance: Shows a debate-then-refine loop helps when the debate ends in retrieval of rules. It does not test story building from messy evidence.

source: Sun et al. (2026) CyberJurors: A Multi-Agent Simulation Task for E-Commerce Disputes Verdict (VerdictBench)
finding: A 17-juror simulation with structured per-juror reasoning and past verdicts as precedent beat single models and court simulators on real crowd-jury dispute data.
numbers: VerdictBench 6,000 real cases; sellers win 62.6%, buyers 37.4%. Accuracy gains: +9.48% over LLMs, +9.38% over MLLMs (and over best single model Gemini-3-Pro), +6.19% over court simulators. Text-only LLMs averaged 55.78% vs MLLMs 52.98%. Individual Verdict chain-of-thought: 4 stages (understanding, perception, analysis, verdict). Court simulators beat Gemini-3-Pro by 3.19%.
limits: E-commerce disputes, majority vote of 17, not criminal law. Gains from jury and precedent parts are bundled in the ablation.
agent_relevance: One of few cases where simulated deliberation plus precedent helps. Note it uses precedent anchors and structure, not free discussion, which fits our operators.

source: Fu et al. (2026) VeriScene: Reconstructing Crime Scenes from Legal Evidence via World-Model Agent
finding: An agent fuses photos and witness statements into a narrative with a citation for every claim, then runs an audit loop that catches uncovered evidence and contradictions before rendering. It is a coded story-coverage check.
numbers: 139 photos, 65 statements, 25 scenarios, 20 test scenes. Evidence coverage 0.9014, factual consistency 0.7217. +20.35% factual consistency and +34.88% temporal coherence over end-to-end MLLM baseline; baseline has zero coverage by construction (no citations). Without the fusion audit, coverage falls 0.9014 to 0.8436. Cost $1.82 per scene.
limits: Synthetic or curated scenarios; visual rendering quality not the target of the audit.
agent_relevance: Closest working agent version of the story model's coverage criterion: cite every evidence item, then audit the gaps. Uses code to count citations. Fits S7 scoring.

source: Wu et al. (2026) JuryBench (positioning against prior work)
finding: The paper says earlier LLM court simulators work from judgments already written, so facts are conclusive and defendants only repeat remorse. This limits what they say about story formation.
numbers: Cites AgentsCourt (He 2024) and AgentCourt (Chen 2025) as civil-law, rule-focused simulators. JuryBench built 500 cases with fixed evidence and varying defendant backgrounds.
quote: the focus shifts to storytelling and emotional persuasion of the jury
limits: Authors' framing; they did not test the story model by name.
agent_relevance: Notes that no LLM study yet tests Pennington and Hastie's three stages directly. A gap and a chance for a small test in our logs.

source: Search record 2026-11-09 (arXiv title, abstract and full-text search)
finding: No paper found that tests the story model itself on language models: no study of story building, story ordering, story completeness, or story-versus-evidence-order manipulation. Checked arXiv searches for story, narrative, scenario, evidence order, juror, jury, CourtReasoner.
numbers: Searches returned 0 papers on narrative/evidence order in law and LLMs; one jury list of 73 hits showed only the studies recorded here. CourtReasoner and Llms on Trial (ICLR 2026) are cited in JuryBench but not opened.
limits: Search budget exhausted (WebSearch, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all rate limited). Absence of evidence in this session only; other agents or databases may hold more.
agent_relevance: Any claim that scoring on whole stories helps a model has to come from our own logs. Treat as untested [D].

source: Ersoz (2026) 12 Angry AI Agents (interpretation limits)
finding: The paper links the anchoring to alignment training, but the design cannot separate that from persona fixing or model family. It also notes persona consistency may itself cause anchoring.
numbers: Two models only. Paper cites Suri 2024 and Echterhoff 2024 on LLM anchoring, Du 2023 and Liang 2023 on debate.
limits: Rival explanations: persona loyalty, temperature 0.9, prompt design, the vote every 12 turns, and the early stop rule that labels stagnation as hung.
agent_relevance: Caution when quoting the 94% hung rate: it measures this setup, not models in general.

source: Bertalanic and Fortuna (2026) Cost of Consensus (communication density)
finding: Conformity sets in after two agents and gets worse with more rounds; more agents did not help. Temperature change did not fix it.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B: modal sycophancy at 2 agents 69.4% vs 73.4% at 9 (GSM-Hard); MMLU-Hard 77.2% at 2 to 85.5% at 9. Accuracy never exceeded self-correction at any density. At temp 0.7, round-1 consensus fell 3.1 (MMLU-Hard) and 8.9 points (GSM-Hard), yet final consensus was statistically unchanged.
limits: One anchor model for the sweeps. Holm-Bonferroni would make the two Llama comparisons non-significant.
agent_relevance: Adding more voices or higher temperature does not buy independence (G4). Keep independent-attempt count small and check with code.

source: Wynn et al. (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap (mechanism notes)
finding: The paper tests three reasons for bad flips: sequential revision, social influence and sycophancy. It reports that the social effect dominates.
numbers: Figure 3 caption: agents that resist flipping a correct answer in round 1 resist less under disagreement in round 2. Figure 4: flip-to-wrong rises with the number of agreeing agents. Reward-for-correct prompt tested as a fix (Section 6).
limits: Table values not transcribed.
agent_relevance: Prompting for reward on correctness was tried as a remedy. Fits the schema rule that prompts are weak levers; checks are stronger.

source: Kumarappan and Mujoo (2026) Not Just RLHF (dissenter rescue and plausibility)
finding: The model counts only plausible consensus. '3 out of 3' worked better than '100 out of 100'. A degraded dissenter still helped, and a mimicry attack on the dissent worked partly.
numbers: c_3of3 yield 82.25% vs c_100of100 64.75%; c_4of3 54.50%; bare declarative line with no jury 64.00%; 'one model' source 40.25%. Dissenter rescue 3v0 to 2v1 over 50 points in all three framings; residual 2v1 yield user-role 5.25%, assistant-role 24.50%, tool-role 44.25%. Adaptive attacks added: weak dissenter +8.50 (user), +19.75 (assistant), +23.25 (tool) points.
limits: Mechanistic claims rest on activation patching in one 8B model. Behavioural numbers use pre-written text.
agent_relevance: Even a lone bare sentence moves two thirds of answers. If any step takes text from a peer or a prior stage, mark its source and keep a dissent slot.

source: Hao et al. (2026) Not All Flips Are Conformity (mitigation)
finding: A predictor that stopped likely adopters suppressed harmful and helpful adoption alike and gave no detectable accuracy gain. When a correct peer answer existed, correction beat harmful adoption.
numbers: Four multiple-choice benchmarks with GPT-4o; selected checks on DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3-Plus. Answer-agnostic intervention: no detectable accuracy gain.
limits: Rates are model-specific.
agent_relevance: Blocking peer influence wholesale also blocks the good part. Better to gate revision on a failing check than to gate on who agreed.

source: Jagged Judges (2026) mechanical vs epistemic stability
finding: Judges that were stable under formatting changes were not stable under argument pressure. Stability under one type does not predict the other.
numbers: Nine judges cluster at 2-9% mechanical wiggle (Claude Opus 2%, Grok-4.1 Reasoning 9%). GPT-5 flips on first challenge turn 32%, Claude 4.6 Sonnet 26%, Gemini 3.1 Pro 7%, Grok-4.1 9%. L1-L3 cluster near 80% retention and barely move after turn 2.
limits: Judge tasks, not trials. Observer model GPT-5 parses verdicts.
agent_relevance: Test the scorer for pushback separately from the test for noise. A stable scorer on reruns can still fold when asked 'are you sure'.
